Leadership · Bhagavad Gita · 6 min read

Don't Be Too Nice

Steve Jobs gave Indra Nooyi three hours and one blunt instruction. Most people hear it as permission to be a jerk. It isn't.

PaddySpeaks · August 2026
The meeting

She called him. He picked up.

Newly appointed to run PepsiCo, Nooyi reached out to Jobs — not for a turnaround playbook, but to understand how he actually ran Apple. They talked for close to three hours.

Almost nothing he said was about strategy. It was about attention: where a leader points it, how visibly, and what happens to a company when everything gets pointed at equally.

What he told her

Four instructions

None of them are complicated. All of them are uncomfortable to actually do.

Pleasant is not the same as clear. If you react identically to everything, your team has no signal to steer by.

Reports are compressed reality. Compression drops exactly the detail you needed.

If it matters, it gets a seat at the table — not a service ticket after the decisions are made.

He told the woman selling soda to cut the sugar. Hard advice is the only kind worth three hours.

At work

Five takeaways for leaders

What the advice looks like on a Tuesday, in a real org, with real politics.

01

Get real

Hierarchy is a convenience, not a shield. Every layer between you and the work is a layer of editing — and people edit toward good news.

Go where the rubber meets the road. Ask. Listen. Then decide.

Take away: Decisions made at the top only count if they survive at the bottom.
02

Show your conviction

This is the real content of "don't be too nice." Jobs wasn't recommending cruelty; he was pointing out that constant equanimity is a communication failure.

Teams read your energy long before they read your memo.

Take away: If everything gets the same reaction from you, nothing is important.
03

Challenge comfort

Consensus feels like alignment. Often it's just fatigue. The ideas worth funding tend to arrive with friction attached.

Push back on anything that serves the org chart instead of the mission.

Take away: Better to disagree early than to regret late.
04

Prioritize what matters

Not everything deserves equal time, money, or your face in the room. Spreading resources evenly is the most polite way to fund nothing properly.

Take away: Saying yes to priorities means saying no to the rest — out loud.
05

Build for the long term

Quarterly applause is rented. Nooyi spent years reshaping a portfolio while being told, loudly, to stop.

Take away: Results are rented. Impact is owned.
Off the clock

Five takeaways for a stronger personal life

The same advice, minus the org chart. This is where it gets harder.

01

Know your worth

People calibrate to the standard you enforce, not the one you deserve. Over-explaining your value is the fastest way to devalue it.

Take away: Self-respect is the silent standard everyone else reads.
02

Show your conviction

Silence held long enough stops reading as patience and starts reading as agreement. Say it clearly, say it calmly, say it once.

Take away: Your voice is your boundary.
03

Set boundaries

A boundary isn't a wall; it's a filter. It decides what gets access to your time, energy and peace — which is the entire supply you have.

Take away: Boundaries today, peace tomorrow.
04

Call a spade a spade

Sugarcoating buys quiet now and pays for it later, with interest. Name the issue, address the issue, keep the person.

And be honest about the difference between kindness and unlimited accommodation. Only one of them is a virtue.

Take away: Truth may sting for a moment. Silence stings for a lot longer.
05

Walk away from what doesn't work

You can't grow in a place that drains you, and staying is not loyalty once it becomes a habit. Leaving isn't quitting; it's choosing where your effort lands next.

Take away: Close chapters. Open better ones.
The older source

Nishkāma Karma is not doormat karma

The Gita's most quoted verse is also its most misused — usually by whoever benefits from your silence.

"You have the right to perform your actions, but never to the fruits of your actions."

Detachment from reward is a discipline about your expectations. It says: do the work well, don't hold the outcome hostage. It never said everyone else may eat the fruit while you keep watering the tree.

Duty with excellence. Detachment from reward. Neither one requires you to be a doormat.

If you remember nothing else

The whole thing in six lines

  1. Nice is a tone. Clear is a duty. You can be both — but only one of them is your job.
  2. Flat reactions destroy signal. Show what matters, visibly, or watch your team guess.
  3. Go to the ground floor. Reports tell you what happened. People tell you why.
  4. Priorities are subtraction. Anything that isn't a no is quietly a yes.
  5. Boundaries are filters, not walls. They protect the work as much as the person.
  6. Detachment ≠ submission. Give up the demand for the fruit, not your right to the tree.
